blocks.text: Census totals need a mapped collection area. For the 1886 census, the Department of Lands and Survey reported preparing 674 separate census plans. Enumerators used mapped districts and smaller sub-districts to collect returns before statisticians could assemble population totals by place.

blocks.text: By 1901, survey offices prepared and checked district maps for hundreds of smaller collection areas. The census report describes coloured maps for sub-enumerators; 895 people held those roles. Survey offices and the statistics office were already working together to draw, check and assign geography before a census table was published.

blocks.text: The National Registration Act 1915 required men aged 17 to 60 to give the Government Statistician details including name, address, age, occupation, dependants and health. Post and Telegraph staff delivered the cards, and 208,513 men returned them. The register was a wartime administrative record, separate in law from the ordinary census, but it relied on nationwide enumeration and address information.

blocks.text: When conscription began under the Military Service Act 1916, the Government Statistician used the 1915 register and other records to create the ballot roll. Malcolm Fraser administered the ballots and, in June 1918, drew his own card at age 45. That small detail gives the national filing operation a human scale.

blocks.text: For the 1945 census, Lands and Survey staff prepared more than 1,300 enumerator maps, divided into units the reports called “population mesh blocks”. The small areas let population be assembled locally and then aggregated into larger administrative and electoral geographies.

blocks.text: A census area had to be drawn, checked and maintained before a return could be assigned to it. Statistics New Zealand later documented how it defined statistical boundaries while LINZ maintained their digital files on its behalf. Chapter 16 follows the transition from enumerator maps to digital census geography.
